textRegions.tex: 4 In triangle \(ABC,BC=(x+2)\text{ cm},AC=x\text{ cm}\) and \(\angle BCA=150^\circ\). Given that the area of the triangle is \(5\text{ cm}^2\), work out the value of \(x\), giving your answer to 3 significant figures.

Area of \(\triangle ABC=\frac12x(x+2)\sin150^\circ\text{ cm}^2\).\[\begin{aligned}\text{So }5&=\tfrac12x(x+2)\times\tfrac12\\\text{So }20&=x(x+2)\\\Rightarrow x^2+2x-20&=0\end{aligned}\]Using the quadratic formula:\[x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\]\[x=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{84}}2\]\(x=3.582\ldots\) or \(x=-5.582\ldots\).\par As \(x>0,x=3.58\) (3 s.f.).

transcription.tex: (i) The volume of \(OABC=\frac13\times\) the area of triangle \(OAB\times OC=\frac16abc\).\par(ii) Using the scalar product with vectors \(\overrightarrow{CA}\) and \(\overrightarrow{CB}\),\[\sqrt{a^2+c^2}\sqrt{b^2+c^2}\times\cos\theta=\begin{pmatrix}a\\0\\-c\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}0\\b\\-c\end{pmatrix}=c^2\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\frac{c^2}{\sqrt{a^2+c^2}\sqrt{b^2+c^2}}\]The cosine rule \((AB^2=AC^2+BC^2-2\times AC\times BC\times\cos\theta)\) will also yield this result.\par The area of triangle \(ABC\) will be \(\frac12\times\sqrt{a^2+c^2}\sqrt{b^2+c^2}\times\sin\theta\)\[\begin{aligned}&=\frac12\times\sqrt{a^2+c^2}\sqrt{b^2+c^2}\times\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{c^2}{\sqrt{a^2+c^2}\sqrt{b^2+c^2}}\right)^2}\quad\text{(because }\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta)\\&=\frac12\times\sqrt{(a^2+c^2)(b^2+c^2)-c^4}\\&=\frac12\times\sqrt{a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2}\end{aligned}\]So \[\frac13\times\left(\frac12\times\sqrt{a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2}\right)\times d=\frac16abc\Rightarrow\frac1{d^2}=\frac{a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2}{a^2b^2c^2}\]which simplifies to the stated result.\par A similar result is true for the right-angled triangle \(PQR\), in which \(X\) is the foot of the perpendicular from the right-angle \(Q\) to the hypotenuse \(PR\): \(\frac1{PQ^2}+\frac1{QR^2}=\frac1{QX^2}\).

One possible value is \(k=60^\circ\). The curve crosses upwards at \(x=-60^\circ\), where \(x+k=0^\circ\).
b.
Yes. Sine has period \(360^\circ\), so \(k=60^\circ+360^\circ n\), where \(n\) is any integer, gives the same graph.
